in_text_mentions: An endomyocardial biopsy was performed; however, pathologic examination of the obtained specimens revealed mainly thrombus with some necrotic tissue. Despite the biopsy results, a diagnosis of endomyocardial fibrosis secondary to HES was made, on the basis of the imaging, clinical, and laboratory findings, and other secondary causes of hypereosinophilia were ruled out. Despite the team effort and adequate treatment, patient deteriorates to NYHA class IV and died seven days after admission. Then, autopsy was done which confirms the diagnosis of Löffler endocarditis (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: May-Grünwald-Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear from a human patient showing increased eosinophils accounting for ~25% of leukocytes, directly supporting the diagnosis of hypereosinophilic syndrome stated in the caption and in-text mentions. Peripheral blood eosinophilia is not covered by the provided finding vocabulary, so it is listed as a proposed finding. B: Bone marrow aspirate smear from the same human patient demonstrating striking eosinophilic hyperplasia (56.4% of nucleated cells) with a red arrow marking a representative eosinophil, matching the marrow eosinophilia finding for hypereosinophilic syndrome and supported by the case report's diagnosis.

(A) Peripheral blood smear (May-Grünwald-Giemsa stain, ×100 objective) shows increased eosinophils, accounting for approximately 25% of leukocytes. in_text_mentions: Serial blood counts confirmed persistent hypereosinophilia, with the absolute eosinophil count reaching 2.16 × 10⁹/L. Peripheral blood smear examination showed eosinophils accounting for approximately 25% of leukocytes, without circulating blasts. Bone marrow aspiration showed active trilineage hematopoiesis and striking eosinophilic hyperplasia; eosinophils comprised 56.4% of nucleated marrow cells. The report did not describe blast excess, overt multilineage dysplasia, or abnormal megakaryocytic morphology (Figures 3A,B).

in_text_mentions: le cine-MRI images showed a low-signal solid mass at the LV apex and a marked thickening of its attached endocardium (Figure 4B and C). A: Four-chamber cine systolic frame from a patient with hypereosinophilic syndrome and Löffler endocarditis, showing apical endocardial thickening and an intracavitary filling defect consistent with mural thrombus. D: T1 mapping image showing abnormal signal in the involved endomyocardium of a patient with hypereosinophilic syndrome and Löffler endocarditis. E: Fat-suppressed T2-weighted image showing increased endomyocardial signal consistent with active edema/inflammation in eosinophilic endomyocardial injury.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Gross midventricular cross-section of the explanted heart from a patient with hypereosinophilic syndrome; shows the classic obliterative endomyocardial fibrosis (Loeffler endocarditis) of the right ventricle with a nearly obliterated RV cavity, matching the caption and in-text description. LV/RV labels are present. b: Histology of the right ventricular endocardium from the same hypereosinophilic syndrome patient, showing diffuse subendocardial fibrosis with minor calcification, the fibrotic end-stage lesion of eosinophilic endomyocardial disease. He had a longstanding history of eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil counts consistently above the diagnostic threshold for HES) but no known parasitic or systemic disease. On examination, he was asymptomatic with normal vital signs. The ECG (Figure 1) showed left ventricular hypertrophy and widespread T‐wave inversion, findings consistent with those seen in EMF. TTE was unremarkable except for mild diastolic dysfunction. To exclude occult coronary disease and clarify the etiology of these changes, stress CMR was performed.

panels.rationale: Twelve-lead ECG from a patient with hypereosinophilic syndrome with cardiac involvement (article title and in-text description). The panel is a genuine patient recording showing repolarization abnormalities (hyperacute T waves, low voltages, LBBB) and atrial fibrillation, which map to the HES ECG ST-T abnormality finding in the vocabulary. The rhythm/repolarization changes are non-specific and partly attributable to concurrent hyperkalemia (K 6.9), so disease attribution confidence is moderate and typicality is treated as a variant rather than classic eosinophilic endomyocardial disease.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E endomyocardial biopsy panel showing organizing thrombus in small endocardial vessels with eosinophilic infiltrate, consistent with eosinophilic myocarditis in idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome. B: H&E endomyocardial biopsy panel showing an older organized endocardial scar with rare eosinophils and hemosiderin-laden macrophages, representing reparative-stage eosinophilic myocardial involvement in hypereosinophilic syndrome. C: H&E endomyocardial biopsy panel with a close-up of intact and degranulating interstitial eosinophils, a characteristic histologic manifestation of eosinophilic myocarditis in hypereosinophilic syndrome. D: H&E endomyocardial biopsy panel showing a larger cluster of non-degranulated eosinophils, supporting eosinophilic myocardial infiltration in hypereosinophilic syndrome.

in_text_mentions: On the sixth day of her hospitalization, a right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy was done, which showed endomyocardial thrombosis with eosinophilia consistent with EM. Eosinophilic infiltrate was present in the thrombosed area of the small vessels of the endocardium. The myocardium showed a repair process with lingering mononuclear cells, fibroblasts and interstitial collagen. There was no evidence of Aschoff nodules, giant cells or granulomata. A Movat stain showed no evidence of fibroelastosis. There was also no evidence of amyloid (Thioflavin-S) deposition in the interstitium (Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Single-panel figure: Giemsa-stained smear of pleural fluid from a patient with idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (article title: 'Pericardial Effusion and Progressive Bilateral Effusion as Rare Presentations of Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome'). Yellow arrows highlight eosinophils, and the in-text cytology description documents a primarily eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate, matching the HES tissue eosinophilic infiltrate finding. Serosal effusion is a recognized but uncommon (variant) presentation of HES; the stain is Giemsa cytology rather than H&E, so the modality is coded as the closest light-microscopy histology category. No age, ethnicity or skin information is provided in caption or text.

in_text_mentions: Further examination of the pleural effusion at our hospital revealed it to be a serious fluid accumulation, and the results of the loop-mediated isothermal amplification method for tuberculosis were negative. The adenosine-deaminase level in the pleural fluid was also not elevated, and cytological analysis showed no malignant cells and only non-specific, primarily eosinophilic inflammatory findings consisting of a mixture of lymphocytes, histiocytes, granulocytes, and prominent eosinophils (Figure 3).

panels.figure_caption: Multimodality images for the diagnosis of perimyocarditis CMR images demonstrate mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement (yellow arrows) in the basal septum (A, B) and diffusely increased T1 values (C) consistent with the diagnosis of myocarditis. CCTA (D) and echo images (E, F) demonstrate pericardial thickening (blue arrows), in addition to late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) of the pericardium (A), consistent with the diagnosis of pericarditis. Of note, the CMR findings are less pronounced than more fulminant presentations found in the medical literature, which can exhibit subendocardial fibrosis and ventricular thrombi. This case represents an earlier stage presentation with increased T1 values and LGE, which are sufficient for the diagnosis given the clinical context. CCTA, coronary computed tomography angiography; CMR, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
in_text_mentions: infectious evaluations, including antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), parasitic serology for strongyloides, stool tests for ova and parasites, total immunoglobulin E (IgE), and Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE, were negative or within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear did not identify dysplasia, circulating blasts, or other hematologic abnormalities. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) revealed late gadolinium enhancement of the pericardium and focal myocardial involvement, consistent with perimyocarditis given the clinical context (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Low-power H&E bone marrow biopsy from the reported patient (article title: hypereosinophilic syndrome with thrombus); the marrow is hypercellular with a marked eosinophilic myeloid population, matching marrow eosinophilia. Caption itself only describes negative mutation testing, so disease attribution rests on the article's primary diagnosis of hypereosinophilic syndrome together with the patient-specific marrow specimen. B: Higher-magnification H&E of the same bone marrow biopsy, showing a hypercellular marrow with abundant eosinophilic myeloid cells consistent with marrow eosinophilia in the patient's hypereosinophilic syndrome. Arrow annotation present; no ethnicity, age or skin data provided.

panels.figure_caption: Bone marrow biopsy, negative for BCR-ABL1 and JAK 2 mutation (see arrow)
in_text_mentions: thology noted a diminished quantity of platelets. The bone marrow biopsy from the patient’s previous admission was evaluated for JAK2 mutation and BCR-ABL1; additionally, FISH analysis was performed for PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, and core-binding factor subunit beta (CBFB) (Figures 2-3). The analysis was positive for PDGFRA mutation with 50% cellularity consistent with a myeloid neoplasm. In light of the NSTEMI with concomitant eosinophilia with mild thrombocytopenia, oncology was consulted urgently to both evaluate the performance status of the patient and candidacy for dual antiplatelet therapy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Renal biopsy H-E panel showing a glomerulus with moderate mesangial hypercellularity (white arrow); the article title identifies this immune complex-mediated MPGN pattern as a renal manifestation of idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome, and in-text mentions eosinophil cells in capillary lumens. b: Renal biopsy H-E panel demonstrating an interstitial inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophils, a specific histologic manifestation of hypereosinophilic syndrome in this case report of renal HES involvement.
